# PART A - Vectors

#PART B - Subsetting
```{r}
grades <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")

grades[3]
grades[c(1,4)]
grades[c("Science", "PE")]

grades[-c(1,4)]
grades[grades >= 85]

grades[10]

Filter(function(i) { all(i %% c(3,5,7) != 0) }, seq(100))
```
#Question 5
#Describe a real situation where you would need negative indexing, and a different situation where logical indexing would be the better tool.

  Negative indexing is useful when you want to exclude the position of row or column of a dataset. Logical indexing is when you want to filter a dataset of customer transactions.

#Question 6
#What happens if you run grades[10] (an index that doesn’t exist)? Run it, observe the result, and explain why R responds this way instead of throwing an error.

  It returns <NA> with a numeric index of 10 because the vector only has 5 elements.
  
#Question 7
#Print a vector with the integers between 1 and 100 that are not divisible by 3, 5 and 7 using filter option.

  Filter(function(i) { all(i %% c(3,5,7) != 0) }, seq(100))
  
  output: 71 73 74 76 79 82 83 86 88 89 92 94 97



#Part C — Vector Operations and append()
```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
y <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)

x + y

z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
short <- c(1, 0)

z + short

fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry")
append(fruits, "date")
append(fruits, "kiwi", after = 1)



```
#Question 8
#Explain, in your own words, what R’s “recycling rule” did to short to make the addition work.

  The two vectors has an unequal length so Recycling rules automatically repeats the element of the shorter vector until they matches.

#Question 9
#Then try adding z to c(1, 0, 1, 1) (length 4). Compare the warning (or lack of one) in each case, and explain what condition determines whether R recycles silently versus with a warning.

  The longer vector’s length is an exact multiple of the shorter vector’s length. It throws a warning because 4 does not divide evenly into 6, meaning recycling cuts off.
  


  
#Part D — Lists: Creating and Subsetting
```{r}

student <- list(
  name = "Maria Santos", 
  age = 20, 
  grades = c(88, 92, 79), 
  is_enrolled = TRUE
)

student["grades"]
class(student["grades"])
student[["grades"]]
class(student[["grades"]])

student$name
student[["grades"]][2]



```
#Question 10
  student["grades"]             output: NULL
  class(student["grades"])      output: "list"
  
  Single bracket returns a sub-list containing the vector “class”, double-bracket extracts the actual contents in lists, returning numeric vector

#Question 11
#Why do you think R makes a distinction between [ ] and [[ ]] for lists, but a vector only needs [ ]? Think about what a list can contain that a vector cannot.

  Vectors can only hold elements of a single data type however, lists, can contain different types.
  
  

#Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
inventory <- list(
  item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),
  price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00),
  in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

inventory$item[inventory$in_stock == TRUE]
inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$item <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$item <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
inventory


```
#Question 12

# In challenge-1, you combined logical indexing on one vector (in_stock) to filter a different vector (item) inside the same list. Explain, step by step, why inventory$item[inventory$in_stock] works even though item and in_stock are stored as separate elements of the list.

  R evaluates the logical vector expression inside the brackets. Next, it uses positional logical subsetting keeping only the elements where the index corresponds to TRUE.  Even though they are stored as separate vectors inside the list, referencing them together allows R to evaluate vector operations

#Question 13

#Suppose a classmate stores related data as three separate, unconnected vectors (item_names, item_prices, item_stock) instead of grouping them into one list like inventory. What risks or bugs could this create as the dataset grows or gets reordered? Argue for or against using a list (or, later, a data frame) instead of separate vectors.
  
  Storing related data as separate, independent vectors creates risks of data corruption. If you sort, filter, or accidentally delete an element in one vector without doing the exact same operation to item_names, it will no longer line up, leading to silent bugs where prices map to the wrong items. Grouping them into a single list ensures that the variables remain together as single.
  

#CONCLUSION
  Lists are flexible, capable of holding elements of different types and lengths, whereas vectors are strictly store elements of a single data type. You choose a vector when performing mathematical or logical operations. You choose a list when you need to group distinct, multi-type data objects together into a single structure.
